q: 301. The minimum cross fall of shoulders is kept ............
explain: According to IRC standards, the camber or cross fall of the shoulder should be at least 0.5% steeper than that of the pavement, with a minimum value of 3% for earth shoulders.

q: 302. While calculating the sight distances, the driver's eye above road surface, is assumed ............
explain: For design purposes (stopping and overtaking sight distances), the IRC specifies the height of the driver's eye level as 1.2 meters (120 cm) above the road surface.

q: 303. While calculating the overtaking sight distance, the height of the object above road surface, is assumed ............
explain: Unlike stopping sight distance (where the object is 0.15m), for Overtaking Sight Distance (OSD), the object is another vehicle, so its height is also taken as 1.2 meters (120 cm).

q: 304. Curves in the same direction separated by short tangents, are called ............
explain: A broken-back curve consists of two curves in the same direction joined by a short straight (tangent) section, which is generally avoided in good design for aesthetic and safety reasons.

q: 305. The minimum ratio of the radii of two circular curves of a compound curve, is kept ............
explain: To ensure a smooth transition in a compound curve, the ratio of the larger radius to the smaller radius should ideally not exceed 1.5.

q: 306. If V is speed in km/hour and R is radius of the curve, the superelevation e is equal to ............
explain: For design speed (considering 75% of V and neglecting friction), the formula is e = (0.75V)² / gR, which simplifies to approximately V²/225R.

q: 307. The minimum superelevation in rolling terrain in plains, is limited to ............
explain: The maximum superelevation for plain and rolling terrain is limited to 7% (0.07) to prevent slow-moving vehicles from sliding inwards.

q: 308. If the designed speed on a circular curve of radius 1400 m is 80 km/hour, no superelevation is provided, if the camber, is ............
explain: If the calculated superelevation is less than or equal to the road's camber, only the camber is provided. For V=80 and R=1400, the value is low enough to be covered by a standard 1.7% to 2% camber.

q: 309. When a number of hair in bends are introduced, a minimum intervening distance in between is kept ............
explain: For hairpin bends in hill roads, the IRC recommends a minimum intervening straight distance of 20 meters between successive bends.

q: 310. The number of vehicles moving in a specified direction on a roadway that pass a given point during specified unit of time, is called ............
explain: Traffic volume is the number of vehicles crossing a section of road per unit time (e.g., vehicles per hour).

q: 311. The length of the side of warning sign boards of roads is ............
explain: For standard warning signs (equilateral triangle shape), the IRC specifies a side length of 45 cm for normal roads.

q: 312. Enoscope is used to determine ............
explain: An Enoscope is an L-shaped mirror box used for spot speed studies by observing the time taken by a vehicle to cross a short, known base length.

q: 313. The traffic manoeuvre means ............
explain: Traffic manoeuvres include any change in the direction or speed of a vehicle, such as merging into a lane, diverging from a flow, or crossing another path.

q: 314. A road connecting two town is called a ............
explain: Highways are main roads designed for high-speed travel that typically connect major towns or cities.

q: 315. The portion of a road surface, which is used by vehicular traffic, is known as ............
explain: The carriage-way (or pavement) is the specific portion of the road intended for the movement of vehicles, excluding shoulders.

q: 316. The city roads which are meant for through traffic usually on a continuous route are known as ............
explain: Arterial streets are the highest level of urban roads, designed primarily for through traffic connecting major areas of a city.

q: 317. Carriage-way is protected by ............ wide shoulders.
explain: In various highway designs, shoulders typically range from 1.25 to 2 meters wide to provide emergency space and lateral support.

q: 318. In Telford construction, the side portions were made up of only one layer of broken stones and leveled off to give a camber not greater than ............
explain: Thomas Telford utilized a standard cross-slope (camber) of 1 in 40 for the top surface of his road construction method.

q: 319. The camber, for the drainage of surface water, was first introduced by ............
explain: Pierre-Marie-Jérôme Trésaguet is credited with being the first to introduce the concept of camber to improve drainage in road construction.

q: 320. The unit cost of transportation (Au) on a section of the highway may roughly be calculated by ............
explain: The unit cost (Au) is generally expressed as the total cost (A) divided by the product of the number of vehicles (N) and the distance (L), hence A/NL.

q: 321. In order to give satisfactory service throughout the year, the road surface should ............
explain: An all-weather road requires a stable carriage-way, appropriate longitudinal gradients, and a durable wearing surface to resist traffic and weather.

q: 322. The top of the ground on which the foundation of road rests, is called ............
explain: The sub-grade is the naturally occurring or prepared soil bed that supports the entire pavement structure.

q: 323. The foundation of a road is also called ............
explain: In older terminology, the foundation layer providing structural strength is often referred to as soling or the base course.

q: 324. The super structure of a road is called ............
explain: The uppermost layer in direct contact with traffic is the 'super structure,' commonly called the wearing course or road surfacing.

q: 325. When the bearing capacity of soil is poor and the intensity of traffic is high, an additional layer is provided between the soling and sub-grade. This additional layer is called ............
explain: A sub-base is an extra structural layer placed between the sub-grade and base course to distribute loads and prevent sub-grade soil from entering the base.

q: 326. The thickness of base, in no case, should be more than ............
explain: For efficient compaction and structural performance, individual base course layers are typically limited to a maximum thickness of 20 cm.

q: 327. The highest point on road surface is called ............
explain: The crown is the highest point of the transverse section of the road from which the surface slopes down toward the edges.

q: 328. The road surfacing should be ............
explain: To protect the lower layers and handle traffic, the surface must resist water penetration (impervious), withstand wear (durable), and maintain its shape under load (stable).

q: 329. The slope of the line joining the crown and edge of the road surface is known as ............
explain: Cross-fall, cross-slope, and camber are all terms used to describe the transverse slope provided for drainage.

q: 330. The thickness of road surfacing depends upon the ............
explain: Pavement thickness design considers the load (type/intensity of traffic) and the structural properties of the materials used.

q: 331. The main object of providing a camber is ............
options: to make the road surface impervious
to make the road surface durable
to drain off rain water from road surface, as quickly as possible
explain: While it contributes to durability, the primary functional reason for camber is to ensure quick drainage of surface water to prevent skidding and seepage.

q: 332. In scanty rainfall areas, the camber provided will be ............
explain: Since there is less water to drain, a flatter (gentler) camber can be used, which is more comfortable for high-speed travel.

q: 333. On Kankar road, the camber generally provided is ............
explain: Kankar (gravel-like) roads have a rougher surface than bitumen, requiring a steeper camber like 1 in 24 to 1 in 30 for effective drainage.

q: 334. The shape of the camber provided for cement concrete pavement is ............
explain: Straight-line cambers are preferred for concrete pavements because they are easier to construct and maintain with rigid slabs.

q: 335. A barrel camber consists of ............
options: two straight slopes joining at the centre
two straight slopes with a parabolic crown in the centre
a continuous curve either parabolic or elliptical
explain: A barrel camber features a continuous, smooth curve across the entire width of the road, usually parabolic in shape.

q: 336. A camber consisting of two straight slopes joining at the centre is called ............
explain: A sloped camber consists of two linear planes meeting at the crown, creating a simple 'V' or roof shape.

q: 337. The camber of road should be approximately equal to ............ the longitudinal gradient.
explain: As a general rule of thumb for drainage, the cross slope (camber) is often half the value of the ruling longitudinal gradient.

q: 338. Super-elevation is expressed as ............
options: the difference of heights of two edges of the carriage-way to the width of the carriage-way
the difference of radii of curves
the difference of the road gradients
explain: Superelevation (e) is defined as the ratio of the height of the outer edge above the inner edge (h) to the horizontal width of the pavement (W).

q: 339. The main advantage of providing super-elevation is ............
options: to decrease the intensity of stresses on the foundation
to increase the stability of the fast moving vehicles, when they negotiate a horizontal curve
to achieve higher speed of vehicles
explain: Superelevation counteracts centrifugal force, keeping vehicles stable at higher speeds and preventing uneven stress on the road base.

q: 340. In the absence of super-elevation on road along curves, pot holes are likely to occur at the ............ of the road.
explain: Without superelevation, centrifugal force pushes vehicles toward the outside, causing excessive pressure and wear on the outer edge, leading to pot holes.

q: 341. The super-elevation is ............
options: directly proportional to the velocity of vehicles
inversely proportional to the velocity of vehicles
directly proportional to the width of pavement
inversely proportional to the width of pavement
explain: From the formula $e = V^2 / (gR)$, it is clear that required superelevation increases as the square of the velocity (V).

q: 342. If the width of carriage way is 10 m and the outer edge is 40 cm higher than the inner edge, then the super-elevation required is ............
explain: Superelevation = Height / Width = 0.4m / 10m = 0.04. Converting to '1 in X' format: 0.04 = 1/25, so 1 in 25.

q: 343. The rate of rise or fall of the road surface along its length, is called ............
explain: Gradient refers to the longitudinal slope of the road, representing the rise or fall per horizontal distance along the road's alignment.

q: 344. Superelevation balances the centrifugal force corresponding to ............
explain: IRC recommends designing superelevation to balance the full centrifugal force for 75% (three-fourth) of the design speed, assuming friction is zero.

q: 345. The gradient of a road depends upon the ............
explain: Gradient choice is influenced by the terrain (ground), the pulling power of vehicles (traffic), and drainage requirements (rainfall).

q: 346. The steepest gradient which is to be permitted on the road is called ............
explain: The 'Maximum' or 'Limiting' gradient is the steepest slope allowed by an engineer for short stretches where ruling gradients aren't feasible.

q: 347. The value of maximum gradient for hill roads is ............
explain: For hill roads in steep terrain, the ruling gradient is typically 1 in 20 (5%), while the limiting gradient can go steeper.

q: 348. The suitable gradient within which the engineer must endeavour to design the road is called ............
explain: The ruling gradient is the ideal maximum gradient that a designer tries to stay within for the majority of the road's length.

q: 349. The total rise or fall between any two points chosen on the alignment divided by the horizontal distance between the two points, is called ............
explain: Average gradient is calculated by taking the net elevation difference and dividing it by the total horizontal length.

q: 350. Exceptional gradient should not be provided in a length more than ............
explain: Exceptional gradients are very steep and are limited to short lengths (maximum 100 m) to prevent vehicle engines from overheating or stalling.

q: 351. The distance, measured along the centre line of a road, over which a driver can see the opposite object on the road surface, is called ............
explain: Sight distance is the length of the road visible ahead to the driver at any instance. It is measured along the centerline of the road.

q: 352. The stopping sight distance is the ............ of reaction distance and the braking distance.
explain: SSD = Lag Distance (distance traveled during reaction time) + Braking Distance (distance traveled after applying brakes).

q: 353. The stopping sight distance depends upon the ............
explain: SSD is influenced by the total reaction time of the driver, the speed of the vehicle, and the efficiency of the brakes (braking distance).

q: 354. The reaction time of a driver ............ with the increase in speed.
explain: As speed increases, drivers tend to be more alert, effectively decreasing their reaction time compared to low-speed driving where they might be more relaxed.

q: 355. The stopping sight distance is always ............ overtaking sight distance.
explain: Stopping sight distance is the minimum distance required to stop, while Overtaking Sight Distance requires much more length to safely pass another vehicle.

q: 356. The opportunities to cross slow moving traffic at intervals is not provided in case of ............
explain: On two-lane highways without extra passing lanes or adequate OSD, drivers have limited opportunities to pass slow-moving vehicles safely.

q: 357. The reason for providing curves on a highway is ............
options: to provide access to a particular locality
restriction imposed by some unavoidable reasons of land
explain: Curves are used to navigate around obstacles, stay within property boundaries, or reach specific destinations while maintaining a continuous alignment.

q: 358. The factor which influences the design of curves, is ............
explain: Design speed determines the radius, while superelevation and the centrifugal ratio (P/W) ensure stability and comfort during the turn.

q: 359. A horizontal curve on a road provides ............
options: change in the gradient of road
explain: Horizontal curves are specifically introduced to allow a change in the direction of the road alignment in a plan view.

q: 360. A curve whose radius gradually changes from an infinite value to a finite value or vice-versa for the purpose of giving easy change of direction of a road, if called a ............
explain: A transition curve (like a spiral) provides a gradual change in curvature, helping drivers introduce steering gradually and allowing for smooth superelevation runoff.

q: 361. A curve which consists of a single arc connecting ............
explain: A simple circular curve is a single arc of constant radius connecting two tangents.

q: 362. A curve is expressed in terms of angle in degrees subtended to the centre by an arc of ............ radius.
explain: Degree of curve is commonly defined as the angle subtended at the center by an arc (or chord) of standard length, usually 30 meters in road design.

q: 363. A transition curve cannot be a ............
explain: Spirals and parabolas can function as transition curves because their radii change; a compound curve consists of two or more circular arcs with constant radii, so it is not a transition curve itself.

q: 364. The shape of a vertical curve is ............
explain: Parabolic curves are preferred for vertical alignments because they provide a constant rate of change of grade, which is ideal for comfort and sight distance.

q: 365. The rate of change of radial acceleration governs the ............
options: extra width of pavement on the curve
length of the tangent of a simple circular curve
explain: To ensure passenger comfort, the length of a transition curve is designed such that the radial (centrifugal) acceleration is introduced at a gradual, controlled rate (C).

q: 366. In case of a cubic spiral, the polar deflection angle may be assumed equal to ............
explain: For a cubic spiral, the deflection angle (α) is approximately one-third of the spiral angle (φ) at that point.

q: 367. The type of transition curve recommended by the IRC is ............
explain: The Spiral (specifically the cubic spiral) is the transition curve recommended by the Indian Roads Congress (IRC) because it satisfies the requirement of a linear change in curvature.

q: 368. Which of the following is not a transition curve?
explain: A compound curve is a series of circular arcs; it does not feature a transition (gradual change from straight to circular).

q: 369. The intrinsic equation of an ideal transition curve representing a clothoid is given by ............
explain: The spiral angle φ for a clothoid/spiral is given by l²/(2RL), where l is the distance from the start of the curve.

q: 370. The length of the tangent of a simple curve having angle of deflection θ and radius of curvature R, is equal to ............
explain: The tangent length (T) is a basic trigonometric property of a circle: T = R tan(θ/2).

q: 371. Alignment of a road is finally decided on the basis of ............
explain: Detailed field surveys (preliminary and final location surveys) provide the precise data needed to fix the center line of the road.

q: 372. A track of width 1 to 1.2 m constructed along the selected alignment to facilitate access to the area for inspection and detailed survey is known as ............
explain: Trace cut (or trace out) is a small path made during hill road surveys to allow the surveyor to traverse the alignment and verify gradients.

q: 373. The gradients of trace cuts for hill roads are kept ............
options: 10 to 20% easier than the ruling gradient
20 to 25% easier than the ruling gradient
10 to 20% steeper than the ruling gradient
20 to 25% steeper than the ruling gradient
explain: Trace cut gradients are kept easier (less steep) than the final ruling gradient to allow for adjustments during the actual road construction.

q: 374. In detailed survey of a hill road, the interval for plotting the contours at sharp curves is generally ............
explain: On sharp curves in hilly terrain, a smaller contour interval (typically 2 m) is needed to accurately represent the steep changes in topography.

q: 375. The longitudinal levels, in detailed survey of a hill road, should be taken at ............ intervals.
explain: Standard practice for detailed longitudinal leveling in hilly areas often uses a 10-meter interval to ensure an accurate profile.

q: 376. A terrain with cross-slope less than 10 percent, is called ............
explain: According to IRC terrain classification, 'Level' terrain has a cross slope of 0-10%.

q: 377. A curve at the ridge of a hill having a convex shape is called a ............
explain: A summit curve is a vertical curve with convexity upwards, occurring when a rising grade meets a falling grade or a flatter grade.

q: 378. A gradient at which no tractive force is required to maintain constant speed by a vehicle is called ............
explain: A floating gradient is a downward slope that allows a vehicle to maintain a constant speed using its own momentum without using engine power.

q: 379. In hill roads, minimum sight distance required is ............
explain: In difficult hilly terrain, it is often impossible to provide OSD, so the absolute minimum requirement is the Stopping Sight Distance (SSD).

q: 380. In the initial stage of construction of hill roads, no curve should have a radius less than ............
explain: For safety and vehicle maneuverability, the minimum radius for hairpin bends or sharp curves in hill roads is typically set at 20 m.

q: 381. For walls less than 6 m in height, the thickness of the retaining wall at the bottom is equal to ............
explain: An empirical rule for the base width of a gravity retaining wall is approximately 0.4 times the total height (H).

q: 382. A wall constructed to retain the earth from slippage on the hill side of the roadway is called ............
explain: A breast wall is built on the uphill side to prevent the natural slope from sliding onto the road.

q: 383. The height of the parapet wall is usually kept as ............ above the berm level.
explain: A height of 75 cm (0.75 m) is a standard safety height for parapet walls on the valley side of hill roads.

q: 384. The parapet walls are usually required on the valley side of the roadway, in order to ............
options: properly guide the vehicles to the roadway
explain: Parapet walls act as a safety barrier and visual guide for drivers to prevent vehicles from going off the edge on the valley side.

q: 385. The side drains are provided on both sides of the roadway, when the road is ............
explain: When a road is in a deep cutting, water from both side slopes must be collected, requiring drains on both sides of the road.

q: 386. A water bound macadam road is an example of ............
explain: WBM (Water Bound Macadam) consists of crushed stone layers held together by water and stone dust; it behaves as a flexible pavement.

q: 387. A cement grouted road is an example of ............ pavement.
explain: Cement grouted pavements have higher stiffness than flexible ones but less than a full RC slab, classifying them as semi-rigid.

q: 388. The flexible pavement distribute the wheel load ............
options: through a set of layers to sub-grade
explain: Flexible pavements distribute loads through grain-to-grain contact across various layers (surface, base, sub-base) down to the sub-grade.

q: 389. The structure of a road is composed of ............
explain: A standard pavement structure includes the sub-grade (foundation), sub-base, base, and the surface wearing course.

q: 390. The natural soil on which the pavement rests and to which the entire load of structure is ultimately transferred, is known as the ............
explain: The sub-grade is the bottom-most layer consisting of natural or compacted soil that bears the total load of the road.

q: 391. The sub-base course is placed immediately above the ............
explain: The sub-base is the layer directly on top of the sub-grade soil.

q: 392. The wearing course in the case of flexible pavements consist of ............
options: broken stone and granular material mixed with tar
a mixture of bituminous material and aggregate
explain: For modern flexible pavements, the wearing course is typically a mix of aggregate and a bituminous binder (asphalt).

q: 393. The selection of design curve in Wyoming method of flexible pavement design, is based upon ............
explain: The Wyoming method uses a chart-based design that adjusts for climate factors like rainfall, water table depth, and frost.

q: 394. The California bearing ratio (C.B.R.) method of flexible pavement design gives an idea about ............
options: the quality of road making material
explain: CBR is an empirical test that relates soil strength/stiffness to pavement thickness required for specific traffic levels.

q: 395. In C.B.R. test, the value of C.B.R. is calculated at ............
explain: CBR values are determined for both 2.5 mm and 5.0 mm penetration, and the higher value is usually reported.

q: 396. Which of the following method is recommended by I.R.C. for design of flexible pavement?
explain: The Indian Roads Congress (IRC:37) adopts the CBR method for the design of flexible pavements.

q: 397. The group index method of designing flexible pavement is ............
options: an empirical method based on the physical properties of the sub-grades soil
an empirical method based on the strength characteristics of the sub-grade soil
explain: The Group Index (GI) is calculated using soil properties like liquid limit, plasticity index, and the percentage passing the 75-micron sieve.

q: 398. The value of group index of a soil varies from ............
explain: The Group Index formula yields values between 0 (very good sub-grade) and 20 (very poor sub-grade).

q: 399. The minimum thickness of the base of a flexible pavement is kept as ............
explain: A minimum of 10 cm is generally required for the base course to ensure proper load distribution and construction stability.

q: 400. The main advantage of concrete pavements is that ............
options: it offers less resistance to traffic
it is not slippery when clean
explain: Rigid (concrete) pavements are durable, provide a smooth riding surface, and require significantly less maintenance over their long lifespan compared to flexible ones.
